facts.t: For staging, **FDG PET/CT** is the most sensitive imaging investigation for colon cancer diagnosed at colonoscopy, and an **isotopic bone scan** shows the extent of bony lesions in metastatic breast cancer to the bones.

**CT** is the preferred and first imaging modality of choice for all acute head injuries; **infarctions** are demonstrated earlier and are more obvious on **MRI with diffusion**, and **MRI** allows visualisation of a spinal cord astrocytoma with much higher contrast resolution.

CT of the chest is used both as **CT pulmonary angiography** to rule out pulmonary embolism in a bedridden patient with tachypnoea and tachycardia, and as **CT chest with IV contrast** as the next step for a smoker with haemoptysis and a left hilar mass with irregular margins.
**Plain radiography** is least useful in the diagnosis of solid organs and metastatic diseases, while **DEXA** is used to diagnose osteoporosis.
The best imaging modality to diagnose **posterior urethral valve** in a 12-year-old male is **ascending and micturating cystourethrography (ACU)**.
**Cardiac pacemakers** are an absolute contraindication to MRI.
Before a CT scan of the abdomen with oral and IV contrast, the patient should have **normal kidney function**.

Infective and inflammatory lung lesions seen on chest imaging include **lung abscess**, **mycetoma**, **pneumonia** and **bilateral consolidation**, and multiple lesions may represent **septic emboli**; lung parenchyma is viewed on the **CT chest lung window**.

**Lung collapse** is recognised by volume loss and is localised by lobe: total **right** and **left** lung collapse and isolated **right upper lobe** and **left upper lobe** collapse are all seen, with lesions localised e.g. to the **left upper lobe**.

Malignant lung lesions include **bronchogenic carcinoma** (central and cavitating forms), **mesothelioma**, **Pancoast tumour** and **pulmonary metastases**, while cystic lesions include **lung cysts**.
Pleural lesions include **massive pleural effusion**, **pneumothorax** (including **tension pneumothorax**), **haemothorax** and **hydropneumothorax**.

Mediastinal lesions include **lymphoma**, **thymoma** and **carcinoid tumour**; an **air lucency** may represent **pneumothorax**, **pneumoperitoneum** or **pneumomediastinum** (with pneumopericardium or surgical emphysema).

topics.n: Vascular, cardiac and diffuse lung disease

facts.t: Vascular and cardiac lesions include **pulmonary thromboembolism**, which may be accompanied by **pulmonary infarction** and **pleural effusion**, and **aortic dissection**, **pericardial effusion**, **pericardial calcification**, **cardiomegaly** and **pneumopericardium**.
Diffuse pulmonary lesions include **pulmonary oedema**, **emphysema** and **interstitial fibrosis**.
Urinary tract studies include **IVP**, **PUT**, **ascending cystourethrography (ACU)**, **non-contrast CTUT** and **MR urography (MRU)**.

Urinary **stones** are recognised in the **bladder**, the **kidney** (including **staghorn stone**) and the **ureter** (proximal right and distal left ureter), and obstruction may occur at the **PUJ**.
Bladder lesions include **urinary bladder carcinoma** and **urinary bladder diverticulum**, and **renal masses** are reported by side (left or right renal mass).
Congenital and structural renal anomalies include **horseshoe kidney**, **polycystic kidney**, **duplex kidney** and **vesicoureteric reflux**.

On CT, **cerebral infarction** appears as a **wedge-shaped hypodense cortical and subcortical area**; acute infarction is associated with a **positive mass effect**, and **haemorrhagic infarction** is a recognised form.
Infarctions follow arterial territories — **middle, anterior and posterior cerebral arteries** — and **diffusion-weighted MRI** detects infarction earlier than other sequences.
An **acute haematoma** appears on CT as a **hyperdense (white) area**; haematomas are classified as **extradural, subdural, subarachnoid, intracerebral and intraventricular**.

An acute **subdural haematoma** has a **concave inner border**; an acute **extradural haematoma** does not have intra-ventricular extension; **subarachnoid haemorrhage** is seen within the **cortical sulci**.
A **brain abscess** does not have a thick irregular wall, while a **brain neoplasm** does not have a thin regular wall — wall character helps distinguish abscess from tumour.
**Meningioma** is an **extra-axial** neoplasm with a **dural base** and **homogeneous enhancement**; **glioblastoma multiforme** is a **high-grade malignant** neoplasm.
**Herpes encephalitis** has a predilection for the **medial temporal** and **high frontal parasagittal** regions; **meningitis** is another infective lesion to recognise on brain imaging.

The level of CSF obstruction determines the pattern of **hydrocephalus**: obstruction at the **foramen of Monro** involves the **lateral ventricles**, while obstruction at the **arachnoid granulations** involves all ventricles (lateral, third and fourth); hydrocephalus involving the lateral and third ventricles may be associated with **choroid plexus papilloma**.
**Multiple sclerosis** appears as **small lesions perpendicular to the ventricular margins** in the brain and as **small eccentric lesions** in the spinal cord.
Advanced MR techniques in neuroradiology include **MR spectroscopy** and **MR perfusion**, and vascular lesions to recognise include **aneurysm** and **arteriovenous malformation**.
**X-ray mammography** is the **best screening modality for breast cancer above 40 years of age**.
**Digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT)** is a recent advance in mammography that uses **multiple slices to remove superimposed shadows** and gives **better delineation of lesion margins**.

**Contrast-enhanced digital mammography (CEDM)** is a recent advance in mammography: **IV contrast is injected** before the study, images include **low-energy and recombined (subtracted)** images, and **malignant lesions usually show intense contrast enhancement**.

topics.n: Breast masses, calcifications and nodal disease

facts.t: A **spiculated mass** on mammography is **malignant**; a **circumscribed mass** may prove to be a **cyst on ultrasound**, while a well-defined mass may appear **solid on ultrasound**; mammography may also show **asymmetry**, and a **malignant mass** may be shown on ultrasound.
Malignant breast disease may show a **malignant mass on a CC view mammogram** and involve the **axillary lymph nodes**, seen on mammography or as a **malignant axillary lymph node**.
**Malignant calcifications** are **clustered microcalcifications**, usually having a **segmental distribution**; **pleomorphic clustered calcifications** are not a typical benign pattern.

topics.n: Breast MRI, nuclear studies and other modalities

facts.t: On **dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI** of the breast, a malignant lesion may show **marginal enhancement**; **dynamic MRI** is the best modality in the **post-operative breast**, and an **MRI breast study** may show a well-defined mass.

Isotopic study of the breast comprises **PET/CT and PEM**; **PEM is dedicated to the breast**, while **PET is a whole-body study used for distant metastases**; **PET/CT** (axial slices) and a **CT scan of the chest** including the breast are also used in breast assessment.

**Acute pelvic pain** is **non-cyclic pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis lasting less than three months**; in a married woman of child-bearing age the first diagnosis to exclude is **ectopic pregnancy**, investigated without **CT scan of the pelvis**.
The **primary imaging modality for acute pelvic pain is abdominal and pelvic ultrasound**; if ultrasound is inconclusive the next step is **CT or MRI according to the case**.

Non-gynaecological causes of acute pelvic pain include **urinary causes, acute appendicitis and muscular causes**; **colitis** is not counted among the acute life-threatening conditions; the **primary imaging modality for a suspected urinary stone is X-ray abdomen and pelvis**; and a **non-visualised ovary** is not a typical sign of **ovarian torsion**.
Fracture patterns to recognise include **oblique, spiral, comminuted, impaction, depressed, compression, pathological and stress** fractures.

Named fractures to recognise include **Chauffeur, Colles, Galeazzi and Monteggia** fractures of the forearm and wrist and **baseball finger, scaphoid, boxer, Bennet and torus** fractures of the hand, and the **accessory navicular bone** is a normal variant to recognise.
A **mal-union** is a union problem seen after fracture; inflammatory and degenerative joint disease — **rheumatoid arthritis** and **osteoarthritis** — is recognised on musculoskeletal imaging.

Bone tumours and tumour-like lesions to recognise include **osteosarcoma, Ewing tumour, chondrosarcoma, chondroblastoma, osteoid osteoma, aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumour, enchondroma, non-ossifying fibroma, fibrous dysplasia, multiple myeloma and metastases**.
Oesophageal lesions include **mucosal ring**, **malignant stricture**, **corrosive stricture**, **achalasia of the cardia** and **paraesophageal hernia**.
Gastroduodenal lesions include **gastric ulcer**, **duodenal ulcer** and **gastric mass**.

Intestinal lesions include **Crohn's disease**, **intestinal obstruction** and **Pneumonitis intestinalis**; colonic lesions include **colonic carcinoma**, **diverticular disease** and **sigmoid volvulus**.
Hepatic lesions include **liver cirrhosis**, **hepatocellular carcinoma**, **metastases**, **Budd-Chiari** and **hydatid disease**; also seen are **gall stones** and **chronic pancreatitis**.
Traumatic abdominal findings include **liver laceration** and **pneumoperitoneum**.
